title: Residual assessment after a substantial void
clarityIssues: The interval from the 540-mL void to the current discomfort is unspecified.

cues.why: Only the keyed investigation directly repeats bladder. This is a weak lexical aid rather than an independently decisive flaw.

fairness: Bedside residual measurement is the best offered investigation; the earlier prevoid volume cannot establish the current residual. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The volume chronology does not earn a second consequential inference: deleting both numbers still leaves an obvious bladder scan against renal imaging and culture. First node; its explanation does not explicitly give the subsequent drainage answer.

Review-wide scope: all 35 candidate nodes were reviewed using only their presentation, update, exhibit, task, options and explanation. Key order and author self-assessments were not evidence of quality. Two kept/held and five retire-and-replace source records were noted but not graded. This offline editorial review does not verify sources or confer clinical approval; Melissa Rowland must approve exact clinical versions. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured exam frequencies.
suggestions: Make prevoid/postvoid timing change a credible competing plan, rather than offer three tests whose ranking is unchanged by that history. Do not invent a residual threshold.

title: Symptomatic residual after hernia repair

cues.phrase: Oral hydration before another voiding trial
cues.why: Offering more fluid to a full, increasingly painful bladder is a weak foil even without detailed medical knowledge.

fairness: Catheter drainage is the clear best plan. The symptomatic postvoid residual and absence of traumatic contraindications suffice; the explanation correctly avoids a universal cutoff.
The follow-up is coherent and independently answerable. Earlier feedback focuses attention on retention; the new result triggers an elementary treatment rule, not two difficult decisions.
suggestions: Replace hydration with a credible competing bladder-management strategy and supply the finding that separates it from drainage. Alternatively obtain explicit acceptance of an easy safety-recognition role.

title: Postoperative voiding symptoms with pyuria

cues.why: The culture choice is already underway, enabling nonmedical elimination.
Repeats an already described investigation without a new reason.

fairness: Postvoid bladder assessment is the best listed next test. Leukocytes do not establish that infection explains poor emptying.
The infection competition collapses because culture is pending; formal renal ultrasound has little supporting context. First node; no prior feedback.
suggestions: Keep the pyuria distraction but replace the already-pending investigation with a real competing decision. Make infection-associated symptoms versus impaired emptying consequential.
Use a clear stable state if stability matters, rather than unspecified unchanged recovery values.

title: Large painful residual after anorectal surgery
fairness: Drainage is the single best immediate plan. Tamsulosin may have a later adjunctive role but does not empty this acutely painful bladder.
The update stands alone and follows the scan coherently. A large painful residual directly triggers a familiar rule; observation and delayed medication do not create two consequential steps.
suggestions: Compare credible complete management sequences, with a supported patient-specific discriminator. Preserve urgent symptoms; otherwise request explicit acceptance as easy safety recognition.

title: Low output with suprapubic fullness
fairness: Bladder ultrasonography is the best listed test. Baseline creatinine does not settle the cause of low output.
Fullness, pressure and small voids form a classic recognition pattern. Deleting the creatinine sentence leaves the same answer; renal imaging and culture are weak competitors. First node.
suggestions: Make an actual discrepancy in output, examination or measurement timing change the next plan. A normal creatinine alongside classic retention symptoms is not two-step reasoning.

title: Painful residual after same-day surgery

cues.phrase: Oral hydration before another voiding trial
cues.why: The full painful bladder makes this a readily dismissed foil.

fairness: Drainage is the clear best answer; the observed volume is not a universal threshold.
The update is coherent and stands alone. It repeats the same elementary retention-to-drainage rule as the other drainage siblings.
suggestions: Replace the hydration foil and introduce a consequential supported management distinction, rather than a numerical variant. Alternatively seek an explicit basic-purpose exception.

title: Failure to void after catheter removal
clarityIssues: Postvoid bladder ultrasonography is awkward after the patient has stopped passing urine; a bladder-volume scan after the failed attempt is intended.
fairness: Bedside bladder assessment is the best offered investigation. Prior weak stream reinforces retention without adding a separate decision.
First node. Culture and formal renal imaging have little support in the afebrile lower-tract presentation.
suggestions: Use a test label that fits an unsuccessful voiding attempt. Make the catheter/voiding chronology change a credible next-plan comparison rather than merely reinforce retention recognition.

title: Painful distension after an unsuccessful void
fairness: Catheter drainage is the best immediate treatment. Tamsulosin before relief of acute painful distension is not a close competitor.
The follow-up is coherent and stands alone. It supplies a direct trigger for drainage rather than an independent two-step decision.
suggestions: Compare credible complete management sequences using a consequential patient-specific discriminator. Preserve the warning signs, or seek an explicit easy safety-recognition exception.

title: Imaging colic after limited ultrasound

cues.why: The presentation supplies the disease pathway before investigation of the current pain, reducing the diagnostic inference.
Repeating the just-limited modality without a changed acquisition circumstance is a weak competitor.

fairness: Low-dose noncontrast CT is a defensible best option in this symptomatic nonpregnant adult. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The same familiar colic-to-CT rule answers the item even without the ultrasound history. First node; it does not teach the later metabolic answer.
suggestions: Use a neutral header if stone inference is part of the objective. Make a supported patient-specific protocol or adequacy distinction change the plan; replace unchanged repeat ultrasound with a credible alternative.

title: Prevention assessment after recurrent calcium stones
fairness: A 24-hour urine assessment is the best listed recurrence-oriented test. Normal serum calcium does not exclude every parathyroid disorder, but the supplied facts do not make PTH the priority.
Clearance and recurrence establish a coherent later prevention stage; the node stands alone. It remains recall of recurrent stones prompting metabolic urine evaluation.
suggestions: Test a supported collection-adequacy or metabolic-interpretation problem that changes prevention workup. Normal serum findings against weak culture/PTH alternatives do not create a second consequential step.

title: Colic with dilation and a negative plain film

cues.why: The header preselects the stone pathway.
The unmodified repeat of the unresolved test is easily rejected.

fairness: Noncontrast CT is the best listed investigation; a negative plain film does not exclude a calculus.
The explanation calls the ultrasound incomplete, but the update says only that no cause was visible. Nondiagnostic for the cause is more precise than assuming technical incompleteness.
First node. The extra findings do not change familiar stone-imaging recall into two consequential steps.
suggestions: Correct the explanation's acquisition claim. Make the negative film or ultrasound finding discriminate genuinely plausible next protocols rather than add results that leave the usual answer unchanged.

title: Recurrent stones with normal serum studies
clarityIssues: The later prevention stage is less explicit than in the clearance variants; whether the acute episode has resolved and whether this is a planned later collection are unclear.

cues.why: Pre-eliminates the option repeating culture without a new reason.

fairness: A 24-hour urine assessment is the best listed prevention test. No confident error in that priority identified.

The transition from imaging is plausible, but retrieved stone material alone does not establish recovery or full clearance. Recurrence directly selects the workup; completed culture and normal blood tests weaken the alternatives.
suggestions: Clarify planning versus performing the collection and the recovered prevention stage. Replace the already-completed culture foil and test a specific consequential interpretation.

title: New colic after a prior stone episode

cues.why: Labels the diagnostic pathway before the new episode is assessed.
No changed circumstance is supplied to overcome the nonvisualized distal ureter.

fairness: Low-dose noncontrast CT is the best listed option. The symptom-free interval supports treating this as a new episode.
The same answer follows from classic new colic without the chronology. First node; no earlier answer leakage.
suggestions: Make the old-result/new-episode distinction change a credible competing plan. Keep necessary acquisition facts but do not count their addition as proof of two-step difficulty.

title: Metabolic assessment after cleared stone episodes

cues.why: One competitor repeats the named normal assessment; the novel recurrence-oriented test becomes prominent.

fairness: Daily urine volume and solutes are not established by spot microscopy or the serum studies; the 24-hour assessment is defensible.
The later node explicitly establishes recurrence and clearance and stands alone. It remains a straightforward workup rule with weak culture/PTH competition.
suggestions: Replace mostly completed or unsupported alternatives with credible investigations at the same prevention stage. Use a supported discrepancy requiring interpretation rather than normal findings funneling to the only new test.

title: Colic without hydronephrosis on ultrasound

cues.why: The header supplies the likely disease pathway.
An unchanged repeat of a limited evaluation is a weak foil.

fairness: Absence of hydronephrosis does not exclude a ureteral stone; noncontrast CT is a reasonable best offered test.

The task forces another imaging choice and offers no credible reassurance/observation plan, so the negative ultrasound does not actually test whether the learner improperly uses it to exclude disease. First node.
suggestions: Make the apparent negative study compete with a plausible next plan, supplying the facts that rank it. Do not count limited ultrasound followed by familiar modality recall as two consequential steps.

title: Prevention workup after documented recurrent stone clearance
fairness: The 24-hour urine option is the best listed prevention test. Recurrence and clearance support the stage; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The sequence is coherent and the update stands alone. Normal serum findings do not add a consequential inference against culture and PTH distractors.
suggestions: Vary a clinically meaningful prevention error or collection interpretation instead of names and normal analytes. Make the actual data change a credible competing plan.

title: Persistent pain with unlocalized early pregnancy
clarityIssues: Unchanged pulse and blood pressure do not establish stability without initial values; stability matters when choosing an early-pregnancy unit versus emergency care.

cues.why: Routine care is a disposable competitor beside a symptomatic unlocalized pregnancy.

fairness: Prompt in-person pregnancy-capable assessment is the best listed plan; an empty transabdominal uterine view does not locate pregnancy.

The explanation asserts initial circulatory stability that the visible observations do not establish. The symptoms directly select urgent reassessment with little competing interpretation. Standalone case.
suggestions: Supply current stability/severity observations. Compare credible in-person and serial-follow-up pathways based on trajectory and imaging adequacy; replace routine antenatal follow-up.

title: Tissue passage without prior pregnancy localization
clarityIssues: Current hemodynamic observations are absent, although the explanation claims initial circulatory stability.

cues.why: Not a credible competitor after apparent loss and ongoing focal pain; the meaningful comparison is reassessment versus declaring miscarriage complete.

fairness: Tissue passage and an empty uterus do not establish completed intrauterine pregnancy loss without prior documented localization. Persistent unilateral pain supports reassessment.
Two meaningful steps exist: reject unsupported confirmation of miscarriage, then choose a safe disposition. Current stability must be specified to make the destination fair. Standalone case.
suggestions: Add current stability/severity findings. Replace the antenatal foil with a credible pregnancy-loss follow-up plan while preserving the prior-localization distinction.

title: Falling hCG with new focal pain

cues.why: Routine antenatal care is poorly supported by unlocalized pregnancy, falling hCG and new pain; it is a disposable third choice.

fairness: Stable circulation is explicitly supplied. Falling but detectable hCG does not establish location or dismiss new persistent focal pain; same-day reassessment is the best offered plan.
Two meaningful steps remain: interpret the limited reassurance of the trend, then override scheduled follow-up because symptoms changed. Standalone and coherent.
This high-yield decision is substantially duplicated by the new falling-hCG-reassess node.
suggestions: Preserve the biochemical-versus-clinical conflict but replace routine antenatal care with a credible same-stage alternative. Differentiate this variant from Tessa Morgan by a distinct consequential error or consolidate the duplicate.

title: Pain without bleeding in an unlocalized pregnancy
clarityIssues: Pulse and blood pressure still at their initial values do not establish current stability; those values are unspecified.

cues.why: Routine antenatal care is weak beside ongoing unilateral pain and an unlocated pregnancy.

fairness: Prompt reassessment is the best listed plan; lack of vaginal bleeding does not settle risk.
The explanation assumes stability absent from the supplied observations. No bleeding does not change the obvious persistent-pain referral decision. Standalone case.
suggestions: Establish current stability and replace the routine-care foil. Make trajectory or a real competing follow-up interpretation consequential rather than use absence of bleeding as decorative difficulty.

title: Anatomical assessment after limited pregnancy ultrasound
clarityIssues: Unchanged pulse and blood pressure do not establish current stability without a baseline.
fairness: Transvaginal ultrasound is the best listed anatomical next test. Repeat hCG cannot establish location, although serum testing and imaging can coexist.
The unresolved adnexa prompt the familiar next imaging modality; MRI is a weak competitor before transvaginal assessment. First node; feedback does not disclose later hemorrhage management.
suggestions: State stability and frame the priority precisely without implying that concurrent serum testing is inappropriate. Use a supported imaging-adequacy or serial-assessment dilemma whose interpretation changes the next plan.

title: Hemodynamic deterioration in early pregnancy

cues.why: The task itself favors operative control over serial testing, pre-filtering a distractor.

fairness: Urgent operative assessment and hemorrhage control with concurrent resuscitation is the clear best pathway. Methotrexate and surveillance are not close competitors in this hypotensive deteriorating patient.
The sequence is coherent. For full standalone clarity, restate the documented positive pregnancy test; the update itself omits it and the header says only early-pregnancy admission.
Shock with free fluid is an important safety objective, but the options do not create two consequential decisions.
suggestions: Use a neutral management task and retain the shock findings. Obtain an explicit easy safety-recognition exception, or test a different supported perioperative decision after stabilization. Restate pregnancy positivity for independent display.

title: Reassessment despite a declining pregnancy marker
clarityIssues: Unchanged pulse and blood pressure lack a baseline; explicit current stability is needed for destination selection.

cues.phrase: Routine antenatal ultrasound and clinic review
cues.why: Not a credible response to falling hCG and an unlocalized painful pregnancy.

fairness: Same-day ultrasound/gynecology assessment is the best offered response to new persistent focal pain despite declining hCG.
The two-step biochemical-versus-symptom conflict is meaningful, but duplicates Priya Bennett pregnancy-urgency-3.
First node in Tessa's case; its explanation does not disclose the later liver-disease treatment decision.
suggestions: State stability, replace routine antenatal care and differentiate this node from pregnancy-urgency-3 with a different consequential error. Do not turn a declining marker into proof of resolved risk.

title: Symptomatic tubal ectopic pregnancy with active hepatitis
fairness: Laparoscopic treatment is the single best offered pathway: imaging establishes a tubal pregnancy, persistent pain and a plateau undermine expectant management, and active hepatitis argues against systemic methotrexate.

Two consequential steps remain: interpret the current trajectory rather than the previously falling hCG, then apply the separate treatment contraindication. Active hepatitis is necessary clinical information, not an unfair wording cue.
The follow-up is coherent and stands alone. Prior feedback explains reassessment without disclosing the operative answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy or substantial nonmedical cue identified.

title: Persistent pain after assisted conception
clarityIssues: Unchanged blood pressure lacks a baseline. The record does not say how the previous inability to tolerate examination will be addressed.

cues.why: The named omission directly matches Targeted adnexal ultrasound; missing-region logic can select the key without understanding heterotopic pregnancy.
Together with the acquisition worksheet, this makes retrieval of completed images an explicitly futile foil.

fairness: An intrauterine gestation after assisted conception does not resolve symptomatic adnexal pathology; targeted assessment is the best listed plan.

The worksheet correctly distinguishes unperformed acquisition from missing exports. Keep that truth, but change the options so generic omission matching cannot replace clinical reasoning. Standalone case; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Replace retrieval of known absent images with a feasible competing assessment. Establish stability and a workable reassessment route without key-specific permission language. Require the intrauterine finding and focal symptoms to matter jointly.

title: Infected obstructed collecting system
fairness: Urgent drainage is the single best offered strategy. The obstruction and systemic/urinary infection findings must be combined, then drainage distinguished from immediate fragmentation.

Antibiotics and resuscitation have started, so necessary concurrent actions do not compete unfairly with source control. Stent versus nephrostomy is appropriately not ranked without supporting anatomy.
First node in a coherent staged case. Its explanation does not explicitly give the later definitive-treatment answer. No substantial lexical cue or confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

title: Residual stone after successful drainage
clarityIssues: Retain the ureteral stent and defer stone treatment specifies neither interval nor follow-up; it can mean reasonable temporary planning or indefinite neglect.
Stone size, location, elapsed course and intended timing of definitive intervention are absent.

cues.why: Against discharge or unspecified deferral, the only option explicitly clearing the remaining problem is apparent without subtle reasoning.
Makes removal a caricature rather than a credible monitored strategy.

fairness: Definitive stone management after infection control is reasonable, but the record does not establish ureteroscopy now over planned later intervention. This is ranking uncertainty, not a claim that ureteroscopy is wrong.
The explanation's disclaimer about other definitive techniques does not resolve the offered deferral ambiguity.
The sequence is coherent and independently understandable. Symptom relief versus persistence is high yield, but these alternatives trivialize the comparison.
suggestions: Specify the decision stage and concrete follow-up plans. Supply clinically supported stone factors if ranking removal against passage or delay. Compare credible strategies with explicit stent management rather than indefinite deferral/discharge.

title: Confirming passage after symptom relief

cues.phrase: No later image has assessed the stone or collecting system.
cues.why: Names the missing action and selects the only imaging option without understanding silent obstruction.

cues.phrase: the stone was visible on abdominal radiography
cues.why: Repeats a component of the key. This fact is necessary to justify radiography but adds matching help in the weak option set.

fairness: Ultrasound plus radiography is a defensible follow-up approach for the previously radiograph-visible stone. Pain relief and baseline creatinine do not prove passage.
The task asks which investigations and offers one anatomical reassessment, largely deciding the intended need-for-confirmation question for the learner. Standalone case.
suggestions: Compare credible follow-up plans whose ranking depends on symptom relief, recovered-fragment evidence and prior imaging. Retain radiopacity; replace the named missing-image prompt with neutral chronology.

title: CT evaluation of a postoperative urinary leak

cues.why: The key uniquely repeats excretory phases. A reader can fill the named gap without interpreting drain chemistry or injury site.

fairness: Drain versus serum creatinine supports urinary leakage; flank and retroperitoneal findings make ureteral assessment reasonable. CT urography is the best listed protocol; no ratio threshold is needed.
CT cystography is a credible localization competitor after pelvic surgery. The underlying chemistry-to-site-to-protocol reasoning can be two-step if the literal acquisition cue is repaired.
First node; its explanation localizes the problem without prescribing later reconstruction.
suggestions: Retain truthful acquisition information but describe acquired phases neutrally instead of naming the missing keyed phase. Make leak location discriminate urography from cystography.

title: Reconstruction of a distal ureteral injury
clarityIssues: Time from original surgery to re-exploration and local inflammatory/contamination conditions are unspecified, despite deferred reconstruction being an option.
The explanation calls the distal stump devascularized; the update describes a devascularized segment and a remaining distal stump that cannot be reached without tension. These are different findings.

cues.phrase: cannot reach the remaining distal stump without tension
cues.why: Directly states why the end-to-end competitor fails.

cues.phrase: The bladder is healthy and mobile
cues.why: Combined with the explicit failure of end-to-end repair, closely rehearses bladder mobilization. Keep necessary anatomy but improve the competing decision.

fairness: Reimplantation with appropriate mobilization is reasonable for this distal defect; the tension problem argues against ureteroureterostomy.

After postoperative leak detection, immediate reconstruction versus diversion depends partly on timing and local conditions. Stable circulation alone does not settle this; clinician review is needed rather than an invented timing cutoff.

The sequence follows localization and failed stenting coherently. A standalone update should also identify the postoperative sigmoid-resection context rather than imply a newly recognized intraoperative injury.
suggestions: State timing/local tissue findings supporting repair now versus diversion. Correct the explanation's viability claim. Retain operative anatomy while comparing genuinely plausible reconstructive plans.

title: Short mid-ureteral division recognized during surgery

cues.phrase: two well-perfused ends that meet without tension
cues.why: Supplies the standard end-to-end repair eligibility conclusion nearly verbatim.

cues.phrase: The bladder is distant from the defect
cues.why: Explicitly disadvantages the bladder-flap foil, leaving anatomy-to-label matching.

fairness: Stented ureteroureterostomy is the defensible best repair for this short viable mid-ureteral defect; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The update stands alone and clearly establishes intraoperative recognition. All prerequisites for the key are supplied, leaving little alternative plausibility and no second consequential step.
suggestions: Preserve viability and tension findings but introduce a supported real reconstructive tradeoff. Do not hide necessary anatomy to manufacture difficulty; request a basic-purpose exception if that is the intended role.

title: Bladder leak assessment after passive opacification

cues.why: Only the key uses retrograde; the missing technique is named immediately before selection.

fairness: Retrograde CT cystography is the best listed dedicated bladder-leak study. Passive contrast in a nearly empty bladder does not establish an adequate filling cystogram.
Anatomical localization plus acquisition adequacy can be two consequential steps, but exact missing-technique wording enables a shortcut.
First node; feedback describes study adequacy without disclosing later operative treatment.
suggestions: Describe the actual intravenous acquisition, excreted contrast and nearly empty bladder neutrally. Remove the explicit without-retrograde prompt while retaining observations needed to distinguish excretory imaging from a distended bladder study.

title: Intraperitoneal bladder leak with peritoneal signs
fairness: Contrast around bowel loops indicates intraperitoneal leakage; persistent accumulation with rebound and ileus despite free catheter drainage makes operative repair best.

Two consequential steps remain: localize the leak, then distinguish this complicated course from selected conservative pathways. Observation and percutaneous drainage are real alternatives made less appropriate by the supplied course.
The follow-up is coherent and stands alone. Earlier feedback addresses study adequacy, not treatment. No substantial nonmedical cue or confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

title: Torsion concern despite preserved arterial flow
fairness: Sudden episodic pain, vomiting and ovarian morphology remain concerning despite arterial waveforms. Urgent gynecologic assessment for laparoscopy is best; interval Doppler is a credible false-reassurance error.
Two consequential steps remain: interpret morphology/symptoms against the limited exclusion value of arterial flow, then choose urgent assessment instead of delayed imaging.
The constructed report is sufficient for the report-interpretation task and does not name torsion. Standalone and coherent; no confident clinical inaccuracy or substantial nonmedical cue identified.

title: Inflammatory adnexal collection requiring admission
fairness: The infectious history, examination and tube-ovary collection support tubo-ovarian abscess rather than uncomplicated PID or isolated torsion. Inpatient treatment is best despite stable blood pressure.

Two consequential steps remain: classify the collection, then apply its implication for inpatient versus outpatient treatment. The shared drug list isolates disposition and does not uniquely identify the key by convergence.

The regimen names fit the intended pathway; parenteral treatment is clarified only in the explanation. No dose, duration or drainage cutoff is invented. Standalone and coherent; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Optional clarity refinement: specify parenteral treatment in the inpatient option, with parallel route specificity in the outpatient comparator. This does not change the current best answer.
